doc.title: Wayne Bergeron interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 29, 2020

title: Cush Griffith, learning the show by ear, and Bobby Womack
summary: Trumpeter Richard 'Cush' Griffith's charts went unused as Buddy Miles sang the licks; Bobby Womack also disliked charts, and Rowe agrees on playing by ear.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Well it’s funny you should say that because when we were rehearsing, we were rehearsing to go into the recording studio then go on the road, so there was a record attached to this Buddy Miles thing. When we went into the studio, and this guy named Richard Griffin — Richard Griffith, and his, they called him “Cush.” And he was this really cool guy man and he was quite a bit older than me, and he was the second trumpet player. He used to play with Parliament Funkadelic and he’s on some of the recordings even, you’ll see the name Richard “Cush” Griffith. And he was, unfortunately he had some really horrible drug problems and when we were on the road he was hocking his horns and stuff. And he ended up, he lived in Kentucky and he ended up dying. He had diabetes and he’d gone blind and he passed away. But — where was I going with this, I’m sorry.
We were talking about charts or playing by ear.

Oh yeah. So he did, we had twelve tunes we were going to record. And he’d done charts for six horns. There was two trumpets, a bone, and three saxes. So we were rehearsing them in the studio and they were great. Like they were fun man, and they were voiced great, this guy could write really nice. And then Buddy Miles would show up at the studio, three hours late, and he’d go, “Hey let me hear what you got for this tune.” And we would play it and he goes, “well that’s cool but I kind of hear this.” And then he would fire up the B3 and he’d start singing licks to us. And those licks were the show. We ended up not playing one note of the music this guy wrote. And the stuff Buddy sang was nowhere near as good, you know it was very generic, but that’s how we learned the show. And so there was no music. We had memorized it. And you know I jotted things down on music paper so I wouldn’t forget. You know, but so yeah, I used to play, toured with Bobby Womack as well. And Bobby didn’t like having any charts. If he’d see me writing the music down he’d go, “No, man, you don’t need no charts, man, it’s right here. The charts are right here.” And you know what? There’s something to that. He goes, “Man, how are you going to play music if you’re looking at the music?” It’s more of a street thing you know. And so but he was kind of right man. Because when you take that element out of the way of reading something, and you know it, that — there’s an obstruction that’s out of the way between you and the music. And so I could just © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

concentrate on playing the show and it was great. And thinking on my feet if something changes. What if he goes to the bridge four bars early like he would on a regular basis. I’m not buried in a chart and in the wrong place. I’m going, he’s going to the bridge, you know.

I totally agree. And I’ve been in horn bands like that where people never got rid of the music and you don’t learn your place in it, you don’t learn like my note is the fifth of this chord, you just never really learn that unless you start using the ears.
